title: New technologies, industry and enterprise
needs: Explain what automation is, with its advantages and disadvantages.
Say where and why robots are used in industry.
Describe how a planned workplace layout keeps work flowing.
Define enterprise, start-up, intellectual property and patent.
Explain crowd funding, virtual marketing and retail, cooperatives and fair trade.

doNow.q: What does automation replace on an assembly line?
Give one place where robots are used.
doNow.a: Vehicle assembly lines, packing plants, laboratories or aerospace.
A legal way of proving you were the first to register an idea or invention.

doNow.q: Who owns and runs a cooperative?
doNow.a: Its members: its workers or its customers.

clues: I can be programmed to perform a series of complex movements.
I can work where it's too hot or hazardous for people.
You'll find lots of me on vehicle assembly lines.

chunks.label: New and emerging technologies
chunks.summary: Technology keeps developing to meet people's needs and improve how we live and work.

items.text: New scientific discoveries lead to new materials and products.
Communication, design, innovation, modelling and manufacturing, plus problem solving.
Skilled people, tools, robots and machines combined for efficient output.
Consumers want new and improved products, so more are made.
Getting raw materials and making products uses vast amounts of energy.
Small, regular process improvements: more efficient, less energy and harm.

check.q: Why do manufacturers keep developing new products?
check.a: Consumers keep looking for new and improved products.
Making small, regular changes to processes so they are more efficient and do less harm to the environment.

chunks.label: Automation and the use of robotics
chunks.summary: Machines and robots take over repetitive or dangerous tasks.

items.text: Assembly lines do repetitive tasks instead of people, to meet demand.
Software: computer-based tasks. Industrial: physical tasks.
Repeat complex movements in hazardous, hot or fume-filled places: vehicle assembly, packing plants, labs, aerospace.
Faster, accurate, consistent output. Lower labour costs. Works 24/7.
Job losses. No human judgement. New skills needed to maintain. Costly to set up.

check.q: Give two kinds of place where robots work instead of people.
check.a: Hazardous places, very hot places, or where there are harmful vapours.
Job losses, high set-up cost, no human decision making, or workers need new skills to maintain the robots.

chunks.label: Buildings and the place of work
chunks.summary: The workplace is laid out so work flows efficiently from delivery to the customer.

items.text: Planned from the start so design, manufacture and delivery are as efficient as possible.
Work moves through the building in a logical order:
steps: Delivery depot (goods-in): raw materials and components arrive.
Production line: materials are processed and components assembled to make the product.
Packaging (packing): the product is wrapped and boxed.
Distribution (despatch): the product is shipped to customers.

check.q: Why do companies plan the layout of their buildings?
check.a: So each stage of design, manufacture and delivery is as efficient as possible.

check.q: What happens on the production line?
check.a: Raw materials are processed and components assembled to make the product.

chunks.label: Enterprise
chunks.summary: Spotting a business opportunity, developing it and making it a commercial success.

items.text: Spotting a business opportunity and making it a commercial success.
A new company whose idea could become a profit-making business.
Ideas and inventions belong to the person who created them.
Legal registration proving you were first, so others can't profit from your idea.

check.a: A new company with an idea that could grow into a profit-making business.

check.q: Why would an inventor apply for a patent?
check.a: To protect their intellectual property by proving they were the first to register the invention.

chunks.label: Crowd funding and virtual marketing
chunks.summary: Raising money and reaching customers online.

items.text: Many people each give a small amount, often online, to fund a new venture.
From individuals to venture capitalists, usually for shares. An alternative to a bank loan.
Pledged money is usually returned. Failure can harm the company's reputation.
Promoting through websites, social media, email and search adverts. Hits, clicks and likes are easy to measure.
Selling online to reach a wider audience.

check.a: Raising small amounts of money from many people to fund a new venture.

check.q: Why is virtual marketing easier to measure than print advertising?
check.a: It relies on hits, clicks or likes, which can be counted.

chunks.label: Cooperatives and fair trade
chunks.summary: Businesses that share ownership, or that pay producers fairly.

items.text: Owned and run by its members: its workers or its customers.
Shared interests give members more protection and a democratic voice.
Fair prices, decent conditions and fair terms for producers in less economically developed countries.
Sets a fair, sustainable price so farmers' lives improve. E.g. coffee, cotton, chocolate, fruit.

check.a: Its members: its workers or its customers.

check.q: What does fair trade give farmers and workers?
check.a: Better prices, decent working conditions and fair terms of trade.

keywords.def: Small, regular changes that make processes more efficient.
Machines doing repetitive tasks instead of people.
A machine programmed to make complex movements automatically.
The logical order work moves through a building, goods-in to despatch.
Turning a business opportunity into a commercial success.
A new company that could become a profit-making business.
Ideas and inventions owned by the person who created them.
Legal proof the creator registered an invention first.
Small amounts from many people to fund a new venture.
Promoting products online: websites, social media, email, adverts.
Selling products online to a wider audience.
An enterprise owned and run by its members.
Fair prices, conditions and terms for producers in less economically developed countries.

apply.q: A car factory spray-paints car bodies in a booth full of harmful vapours.
reasons: They can work where there are harmful vapours and repeat the same movements accurately
People can make decisions as they go
Its members share the ownership of the business

apply.q: Two friends have designed a reusable water bottle but can't get a bank loan to start making it.
reasons: Many people each invest a small amount, as an alternative to a bank loan
It proves they were the first to register the invention
It sells products online to a wider audience
It gives producers a fair price for their crops

apply.q: A chocolate company wants shoppers to know the farmers who grew its cocoa were treated fairly.
reasons: Farmers are paid a fair, sustainable price and have decent working conditions
It raises money from many small investors
It speeds up production on the assembly line
Hits, clicks and likes can be counted

oddOne.q: Which is the odd one out?

items.why: The only one about raising money.
The only one about promoting a product.
The only one about who owns and runs the business.
The only one that is a legal process protecting an invention.

order.q: Put the stages of the workflow in order.

quiz.q: Manufacturers keep developing new products because consumers keep looking for new and improved ones.
quiz.why: Demand for new and improved products drives manufacturers to make more.

quiz.q: Turning raw materials into products uses very little energy.
quiz.why: It can use vast amounts of energy, which harms the planet.

quiz.q: What is continuous improvement?
options: Small, regular changes to processes that increase efficiency
quiz.why: Regular small improvements make processes more efficient and reduce harm to the environment.

quiz.q: What does automation do?
options: Uses mechanised assembly lines for repetitive tasks instead of people
quiz.why: Automation lets machines do repetitive tasks that people used to do.

quiz.q: Which type of automation performs computer-based tasks?
quiz.why: Industrial automation performs physical tasks; software automation performs computer-based tasks.

quiz.q: Robots are often used where conditions are hazardous, very hot or full of harmful vapours.
quiz.why: Robots can replace people in places that are unsafe for them.

quiz.q: Which is an advantage of automation?
options: It costs nothing to set up
quiz.why: Machines can keep working around the clock, which increases output.

quiz.q: Which is a disadvantage of using robots?
options: They are expensive to set up
quiz.why: Set-up costs are high, though output is faster and more consistent.

quiz.q: Using robots means a factory no longer needs any skilled workers.
quiz.why: Workers need new skills to maintain the robots.

quiz.q: Where do raw materials and components arrive?
quiz.why: The delivery depot is the first stage of the workflow.

quiz.q: What happens on the production line?
options: Materials are processed and components assembled into the product
The product is boxed and shipped
quiz.why: The production line turns raw materials and components into the product.

quiz.q: A company only thinks about the layout of its buildings once production has started.
quiz.why: Layout is planned from the start, so every stage is as efficient as possible.

quiz.q: What is enterprise?
options: Identifying a business opportunity, developing it and making it commercially successful
Using robots on a production line
quiz.why: Enterprise is about turning an opportunity into a successful business.

quiz.q: What does a patent prove?
options: That the creator was the first to register the idea or invention
That a product is safe to use
That a product can be recycled
quiz.why: A patent is a legal process that protects the inventor's intellectual property.

quiz.q: A start-up is a large, long-established company.
quiz.why: A start-up is a new company with an idea that could grow into a profit-making business.

quiz.q: What is crowd funding?
options: Small amounts of money from many people to fund a new venture
Money paid by the Fairtrade Foundation
quiz.why: Crowd funding spreads the cost of a new venture across many small investors.

quiz.q: If a crowd funding target isn't reached, the money pledged is usually returned to investors.
quiz.why: Backers usually get their money back if the target is missed.

quiz.q: How can the effect of virtual marketing be measured?
options: By the number of leaflets printed
By the weight of products sold
By the number of robots used
quiz.why: Online activity can be counted, so it's easier to measure than print advertising.

quiz.q: Who owns and runs a cooperative?
options: Its members, such as its workers or customers
quiz.why: A cooperative is commonly owned and run by its members.

quiz.q: What does fair trade aim to give farmers and workers in less economically developed countries?
options: Better prices, decent working conditions and fair terms of trade
quiz.why: Fair trade makes sure producers are paid and treated fairly.

quiz.q: Coffee and cotton are examples of fair trade products.
quiz.why: Fairtrade covers exports such as coffee, cotton, chocolate and fruit.

written.q: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages for a manufacturer of using automation.
points: Faster, more efficient production.
Accurate, consistent output.
Lower labour costs.
Can work 24/7 or in a variety of environments.
Job losses in the workforce.
No human input or decision making.
Workers need new skills to maintain the machines.
Expensive to set up.
written.model: Automation makes production faster and more efficient, and its output is accurate and consistent. However, it is expensive to set up, and it can lead to job losses in the workforce.
written.note: 1 mark per advantage (up to 2) and 1 per disadvantage (up to 2).

written.q: A start-up plans to use crowd funding to launch a new skateboard. Explain one benefit and one risk of this for the company.
points: Benefit: many people can each invest a small amount…
…so it gives an alternative to a bank loan.
Benefit: websites and social media reach a large audience of funders…
…so a broad range of investors can back the idea.
Risk: if the funding target isn't reached, the money pledged is usually returned…
…and a failed project can damage the company's reputation.
written.model: Crowd funding lets many people each invest a small amount, so the company doesn't have to rely on a bank loan. The risk is that if the funding target isn't reached, the money pledged is usually returned, and a failed project can damage the company's reputation.
written.note: 1 mark for the benefit and 1 for explaining it; 1 mark for the risk and 1 for explaining it.

written.q: Explain why a chocolate manufacturer might choose to use Fairtrade cocoa.
points: Cocoa farmers are paid a fair, sustainable price.
Farmers and workers have decent working conditions.
Farmers can improve their quality of life.
Producers in less economically developed countries get fair terms of trade.
written.model: With Fairtrade cocoa, the farmers are paid a fair, sustainable price and work in decent conditions. This means farmers in less economically developed countries can improve their quality of life.

written.q: Compare using robots with using workers on a vehicle assembly line.
points: Robots can work where it's hazardous, very hot or full of harmful vapours; workers can't do so safely.
Robots give accurate, consistent output.
Robots can work 24/7, so production is faster and more efficient.
Workers can use judgement and make decisions; robots have no human input or decision making.
Robots are expensive to set up and need workers with new skills to maintain them.
Robots lower labour costs but can lead to job losses.
written.model: Robots can work in hazardous or very hot places, or around harmful vapours, where workers can't safely, and they can work 24/7 with accurate, consistent output. Workers, however, can use judgement and make decisions, which robots can't. Robots are expensive to set up and need skilled workers to maintain them, and although they lower labour costs they can lead to job losses.
written.note: 1 mark per valid comparison point, up to 4.

written.q: A food company is deciding whether to automate its packing plant. Evaluate this decision.
points: Faster, more efficient packing, helping meet increased demand.
Accurate, consistent output.
Lower labour costs, and the line can work 24/7.
Expensive to set up.
Job losses in the workforce, and workers need new skills to maintain the machines.
No human input or decision making on the line.
Justified conclusion, e.g. worth it if demand is high enough to cover the set-up cost.
written.model: Automating the packing plant would make packing faster and more efficient, helping the company meet increased demand, with accurate, consistent output. It would lower labour costs and the line could run 24/7. However, it is expensive to set up, it can lead to job losses, workers would need new skills to maintain the machines, and there is no human decision making on the line. It is worth doing if demand is high enough to cover the set-up cost.

levels.text: Detailed, balanced points on both sides, with a justified conclusion.
Some points, mostly on one side, or a conclusion that isn't justified.

written.note: Tick the points made, then use the levels under the model answer to decide the mark.

written.q: Explain why an inventor would apply for a patent.
points: A patent is a legal process that proves they were the first to register the invention…
…so their intellectual property is protected and others can't make money from it.
written.model: A patent legally proves the inventor was the first to register the invention, so their intellectual property is protected and others can't make money from it.
written.note: 1 mark for the point, 1 for explaining it.
